articles.title: This Ain’t No Party Bus: Movement Lessons From the Brandon Johnson Administration
articles.author: Midwestern Socialist -- Chicago DSA
articles.content: “Election day he shouted ‘a socialist for mayor’ The comrade got elected, he happy was for fair But after the election he got an awful shock A great big socialistic bull did rap him on the block. And Comrade Block did sob, ‘I helped him to his job.’” (”Mr. Block” by Joe Hill) Truck of Thrones One evening in late March 2023, a church leader and I were standing out in the cold dark, waiting for Brandon Johnson. Suddenly an amazing vehicle appeared: A crusty old delivery truck that had been transformed with color, lights, a magnificent video screen, and a killer sound system. Inside were two magnificently gaudy thrones. Across the front was a website address that began “HOUSEMUSICTRUCKING. The chariot of Chicago house music legend DJ Farley had become a fixture of the Brandon Johnson campaign. It was part of the advance team that preceded him to events. It was also one of the most Chicago things ever. The truck was so fitting, because house music is an essential ingredient of what Brandon Johnson regularly describes as “the soul of Chicago.” For those that don’t know, house music is an intensely strange and wonderful genre of electronic dance music that was brewed out of Chicago’s empty industrial real estate, marginalized identities, crates of old soul records, innovation, and intense spiritual dedication to fun. Since Johnson was elected, I have reflected on that vehicle as the symbol of all our hopes and dreams. It seemed like this crusty old delivery truck was transformed into a beacon of joy and hope was a personification of Chicago. It felt like we were putting Brandon in the driver’s seat to carry us into a glorious new future. Brandon said frequently on the campaign trail that he was going to bring the people to “the 5th floor,” and we wanted to get on that party bus with him. “This Ain’t No Party, This Ain’t No Disco, This Ain’t No Foolin’ Around” Unfortunately, Chicago is not a party bus. It’s more like an aircraft carrier which has a large crew and is very hard to turn around. And there are a number of different factions among that crew. One was the long-time staff left over from the patronage systems run by both the elder and junior Mayor Daleys, but the folks left over from that era guard the knowledge of where the light switches are. So you can either work with them or sit in the dark. There were a lot of out-of-touch fake progressives left over from the the Lightfoot administration who refused to get on board with being accountable to the people of Chicago. On top of all of this, Johnson had to onboard the multitudes he brought with him, sometimes having to make grim decisions about who gets off the dock or even out of the water. An old machine faction of the Chicago city council attempted to put together the votes to override Johnson’s ability to pick committee chairs before he even took command. And that incident may have forced him to cut a deal with and offer political concessions and other goodies to some of the more transactional alderpersons. I’m not here to make excuses, but the Brandon Johnson and Zohran Mamdani administrations have little to do with the private individuals Brandon Johnson or Zohran Mamdani. Brandon and I both came out of the radical end of the labor movement, and if you’ve been in that scene more than five minutes, you’ve heard the phrase “don’t third-party the union.” That means the members are the union, and the members are solely responsible for the health and performance of the union. To use another metaphor, when I worked as a union rep, I described myself, the elected leaders, other union staff, and the office as a lawnmower. If I leave my lawnmower out in the rain and it gets rusty so my grass gets high, it’s not the lawnmower’s fault. Even if I can sharpen up my blades, fix my engine, and start mowing, it’s going to be rough to mow tall grass. But if I can get the grass down to a reasonable level, it’s going to be a lot easier to maintain. Another way to say this is that the Johnson administration is the product of a movement that further broke the Chicago Machine. And as the old saying goes, “you break it, you buy it.” So where do we go from here? Do we try to fix the Machine? Do we break it more and attempt to dismantle it altogether? Do we drive it around with the bumper hanging off until we get somewhere? Do we trade up for a newer one? Brandon Johnson himself has very little input into this decision. Actually, no individual makes these decisions. The power in a coalition comes from the participation of its constituent groups. The leaders are the leaders exclusively because they have followers. It’s up to movement to inspire its participants to make good use of the progress we have forged. My central message is that we are not done after we have played our role in an election. There is more to do. Chicago activists have thrown around the word “co-governance” as a utopian idea of how much we can collaborate with an office that is not set up for our values, no matter who occupies it. One movement leader, shortly before going to work for the Johnson administration, said it best. “We have not achieved co-governance,” they said; “we have changed the conditions under which we are organizing.” The Wealth of Swamps “Chicago” is an indigenous word that roughly translates as “stinky onion” – the garlic weed swamp. I’ve always imagined French explorers arriving on the banks of the Des Plaines River in Joliet (a block from my old apartment) and indigenous people selling them on the idea of leaving them alone for now to continue onto “the chicago,” just like a realtor today might try to rebrand a troubled neighborhood they’re attempting to gentrify. However, Chicago was not just a swamp, but a swampy portage path. At the dawn of history, in the early days of boating, if you wanted to travel the continent by water, an important step was to get from Lake Michigan to the Des Plaines River. The Chicago wetlands provided you the chance to do that, depending on the water levels, by paddling part of the way rather than carrying your boat. Archer Avenue in particular, but also Route 66, Ogden Avenue, and the I-55, are the legacy of the swamp path. It’s one of the world’s great primal roads. This pathway led to the canal and a port. That caused the original train lines to link here. The trains and waterways brought the roads and freeways. The cowboys brought the livestock from the Great Plains so it could be processed in Sandburg’s “hog butcher for the world.” And so all the real wealth comes through Chicago. While New York and Boston have a lot of money, you can’t eat money, except by owning a lot of land, debt, and commerce elsewhere. Why should we let these pieces of paper control our lives? California and Florida have produce, but that rots if you can’t move it in time. So how do we access the wealth that flows through Chicago? Who has it now and how do we get hold of it for the people’s needs? The Room with Some People A mayoral election is one small battle in the much longer conflict between those who live in the region and those who own the region. I was at one of many Brandon Johnson victory parties that the Mayor-elect did not attend. The director of the community-based 501(c4) organization hosting the party was nervously texting Brandon’s entourage. “He’s in a room with some people,” the director said. I perked up my ears. I’ve heard Chicago community leaders lay out the myth of a ‘smoke-filled room’ like this. The people who own Chicago, it’s theorized, take the mayor in the room and say ‘We don’t work for you. You work for us.’ These capitalists then say what they want from the mayor and the city, and what they can do to the mayor and the city if they don’t get it. Debt can be made due immediately. Industries can be shut down. This is what we call a capital strike: capitalists deliberately shutting down vital infrastructure or tanking the economy to sabotage a left-wing leader or thwart reform. Several South Side Walmarts were closed down between the election and the swearing-in ceremony. The struggle over government actions and subsidies that helped build these stores had been one of the great struggles (and defeats) of the Chicago social justice movement during the Richard M. Daley administration. Walmart claimed the stores were losing money even though the stores were always full, and the company refused demands to show us the numbers. Many of us saw this as nothing short of a capital strike against the mayor-elect. First We Get the Money The people in the back room intentionally obscure themselves from us, but we must track them down and reclaim our wealth. Almost all of our demands cost money. The budget address is way too late to think about how we’re going to pay for the changes we want. The day after the city budget is done, we need to start a campaign for revenue in the next one. Ready or Not, Here We Come “We should not be on the fifth floor, and I’m speaking my whole heart…we were not ready, because we haven’t been in government long enough to know how government really runs.” ( Alderwoman Jeanette Taylor , December 2023) When one is union staff or leadership, it is tricky to encounter a worksite leader who has bad feelings about the union. Often these feelings are a mix of legitimate grievances and unrealistic expectations. When I was union staff, I would always volunteer to go to sites that were accused of being mad at the union. I can work with any type of anger, but it’s hard to move workers who have fully checked out. I tell such leaders the story of the Caucus of Rank & File Educators (CORE), which is a political faction inside Chicago Teachers Union Local 1 (CTU). When I first met Brandon Johnson in 2013, he was chair of the black caucus of CORE. The sad truth is that most union members in the U.S. do not vote in union elections and likely struggle to remember the name of their union, let alone have any understanding of its structure. Many members, I tell the frustrated stewards, get mad about this issue or another, find some untapped votes and, boom, they’re in office. You could do that, I tell them. But the problem is that the failings of union officers are not always personal failings. The pressures of the office can crack even the most dedicated organizers. Many elected union leaders are not prepared for the pressures of what they’re going to face, and they become much like the leaders they ran against. CORE, however, did not seek control of the union until they had power and knew how to wield it. They spent years connecting to their profession and what the school means – not just to teachers, but to the entire community and the public good. They recruited the late Karen Lewis, one of the most authentic and effective leaders in Chicago history, even if she didn’t come from exactly the same political background or traditions as some of the caucus’s founders. CTU won the 2013 strike because Rahm Emmanuel could not split asunder what years of careful thought, exploration, and intense relationship building with the community had wrought. But Alderwoman Taylor, one of the Chicago city council’s most prophetic voices, was right. We were not prepared for a progressive mayor. We did not have the luxury of time and preparation. We took a shot from the other side of the court and were amazed by the swish, and we thought that finally, after lifetimes of heartbreak, we might manifest all our wishes. Perhaps Alderwoman Taylor is right about one other thing too: Perhaps this was not the type of power we needed to build. In the 1980s, the late Harold Washington was Chicago’s most progressive and first black mayor. Washington’s first term was frustrated at every turn by a racist white voting bloc called the “Vrodolyak 29” during a period referred to as “the Council Wars.” During this period, a 29 members of the city council voted down everything Washington proposed. Perhaps we should have built the “Taylor 29” before we looked for another potential Harold Washington. I’ve spent a lot of time with folks I’ve met on the South Side. They don’t talk much about whether Epstein was murdered, but they will talk your ear off about all the ways they know Harold was. But what do we do with this revelation from Alderwoman Taylor? Yes, it’s better to build a plane on the ground before you’re in the air. We didn’t have the luxury of years of preparation, so here we are. We need to find the energy to build multiple vehicles of power at the same time. Chicago Reader columnist Ben Joravsky, the dean of Chicago movement journalism, regularly points out that Chicago doesn’t like nice mayors . He lays out how often we’ve rewarded the bad behavior of our past mayors with defense and support. We also complain about our mayors being too controlling, but we don’t seem to know how to act when someone shares control and responsibility with others. During the 2024 process to pass the city budget, both supporters and detractors would comment that Johnson had weakened the office of the mayor by “losing control” of the budget process. My response to this commentary was always, “Isn’t that what folks elected him for?” My sense was that he laid the worst-case-scenario budget on the table, and then he made the city council own their own efforts at improving it. I thought that was a genius move. If we’re all invited to the 5th floor, doesn’t that indicate shared responsibility? “Johnson has fiercely defended his handling of the negotiations over the city’s 2025 spending plan, repeatedly referring to himself as the ‘collaborator in chief’ and disputing suggestions that City Hall has been engulfed in chaos, even as he called on members of the city council to ‘grow up’ and stop throwing tantrums…not only did Johnson’s original budget proposal ask alderpeople to put their political futures at risk by voting for the largest property tax hike since 2016 and the second-largest in Chicago history, but it offered nearly nothing in return for city council members to point to when speaking to angry Chicagoans.” ( WTTW: “Chicago City Council Narrowly OKs Johnson’s $17.1B Budget That Hikes Taxes by $165M ”, Heather Cherone, December 16, 2024 ) Experience Newark at O’Hare We are electing nice guys who want to be accessible to everyone, but that’s the same thing as being accessible to no one. There is too much noise and not enough signal in this approach. It causes a lack of transparency – or, at least, there’s no transparency about who is getting the access that matters. It’s nice to get attention, but it’s more vital to know early on about what logistics facility, quantum computing campus, stadium, etc., might get built on top of your neighborhood. A picture with the mayor is nowhere near as exciting as having a point person that you know will bring your issues to the mayor. There needs to be an organized way to get ideas, concerns, and information to not just the mayor but the administration. In the documentary Punch 9 for Harold Washington , there’s a scene where folks tell the story of how many ‘no-show’ city jobs they found after Harold was sworn in – corrupt arrangements in which city officials gave jobs to supporters and friends that didn’t require them to do meaningful work. So there’s a real reason to make sure people are at City Hall performing their jobs. But we also need to make sure that the real jobs are sustainable. My friends who work at City Hall look so dead inside. We need to get them fresh air, but we also need to maintain a consistent presence in all neighborhoods throughout the city. If too much governing is happening in one building and not in the neighborhoods, it will never be satisfying. There are so many coalitions pursuing so many separate campaigns, and they’re all trying to get through the city council as quickly as possible. Progressive alders take meeting after meeting with different groups wanting them to champion similar but different causes, with no clear mandate about what to tackle first. The movement needs to pick what will have the biggest impact and has the most organized people behind it. But the administration also needs to communicate on their end. If a community leader has spent their lives developing civic infrastructure in their neighborhood, I should not be the one telling them substantial news about their neighborhood; neither should they first hear about it from the media. In fact, they should know about what’s coming, because they should be involved in shaping it. There needs to be a legion of staff who are constantly listening to and engaging the ‘grasstops,’ who, through the moral authority of their hard work, run the civic life of the city. By ‘grasstops’ I mean the block captains, civic associations, campaign volunteers, church deacons, etc. – everyone that is putting in the effort to make the community life of Chicago happen. We can’t knock on every door, but every neighborhood has people that almost every household engages with. Not Here for Friendship Some social justice activists want to elect mayors and support them by never criticizing them publicly and waiting on them for direction. Some on the left want to constantly form a black-and-white assessment of a leader and either blindly follow or viciously attack them. The situation is much more complex than that. For any of these officials to have successful administrations, the coalitions that elected them need to temper these tendencies. Movements need to independently continue to make their demands. But also, we need to have a reasonable understanding of and strategy around the real limits of the office and the tough decisions that need to be made. We should not be afraid to be far ahead of the mayor but we should not consume our own tail by having unrealistic expectations of the office. We do not live in a world of what is right and just. We live in a world of what is possible with the power we have built. We also do not need to burden the mayor with making decisions that we should be making, and we should not hesitate to be aggressively useful to the administration. We should not hesitate to make moves that perhaps the mayor cannot make as easily. I know one organizer who jumped into being aggressively useful as soon as the election was over. If they knew something, they said something. If someone was angry at the Mayor, they helped his office know about and understand it. Pretty soon, calling them was on the to-do list of new staff. The administration has a lot to pay attention to, and both the organizer and the administration would have both been weakened if they had waited to be asked. Everybody Everybody Sent “Is a tractor bad? Is the power that turns the long furrows wrong? If this tractor were ours it would be good – not mine, but ours.” (John Steinbeck, The Grapes of Wrath ) After the election, a number of voices disparagingly and increasingly referred to the CTU and IFT/AFT Local 1 as “the New Machine.” The old Chicago political machine was the transactional and tightly controlled system in which a small number of people exchanged their political support for city jobs and other perks. Our trauma from living under the old machine can easily make us cynical about any machine or system of organization. Ultimately, whatever your politics, that type of machine is stronger than people who do the minimum amount for the maximum benefit and who are too afraid of the boss to act independently. Hopefully, we will put more into building an open, transformational machine that delivers for the region’s people by making deep structural changes, and less into critiquing individual candidates. articles.title: Capitalism Is Killing an American Cinema Renaissance
articles.author: Jonah Gardner
articles.content: It’s been an exciting year to be a movie fan. After years of declining public interest in the art form, 2026 has brought the movies back in a big way. Just in the last few months, audiences turned their backs on the cookie-cutter, IP-fueled likes of Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu , Moana , and Supergirl , while embracing original films by new voices like The Drama and Obsession . Simultaneously, the rise of repertory theaters has been a lifeline to embattled independent cinemas across the country, while introducing young moviegoers to the pleasures of classic and foreign cinema. On any given night in Los Angeles, James Cameron might show up to a 70mm screening of Aliens , or maybe Michael Mann will be at your local repertory to introduce a new cut of his 1986 classic thriller Manhunter . And then there’s The Odyssey . Whether you love or hate Christopher Nolan’s three-hour blockbuster, it’s impossible for film nerds not to be stirred by the stories of this movie’s wide-ranging success. From sold-out 2 a.m. screenings to debates over the nuances of adaptation, The Odyssey has returned filmmaking to the center of pop culture in a way that few movies have been able to do in recent years. The success of The Odyssey is also a success for IMAX. In the 1950s and ’60s, faced with the threat of television, movie studios turned to emerging technologies like VistaVision and CinemaScope to lure audiences back to theaters with the promise of sharper and bigger images. Today IMAX is serving the same function, promising a beautiful, massive, and clear picture that is far superior to what even the best 4K televisions can provide. A large-scale literary adaptation, instead of a comic book or legacy sequel, whose biggest selling point is the name of the director, should be a positive omen for the future of filmmaking. But even as the industry gathers to celebrate the success of The Odyssey , there are troubling signs ahead. Earlier this summer, the Wall Street Journal reported that IMAX was exploring a sale. Along with the ongoing drama around the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger, an ownership change at IMAX would threaten to disturb the delicate ecosystem of cinema’s resurgence, risking the shattering of a fragile moment that finds itself heavily leveraged in the future of the premier format. A mix of crazy demand, new ownership, and corporate greed could mean that we look back on this moment not as the first spark of a new age of moviegoing, but the last gasp of a dying industry. How IMAX Conquered the Multiplex IMAX was created in the 1960s as a new system for running 70mm film through a camera. The goal of the format was to expose more of the film’s surface area per frame to create a larger, higher-resolution picture. It first caught on for use in science documentaries like To Fly! (1976) for the Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum and The Dream Is Alive (1985) shot entirely by astronauts in zero gravity. Giant IMAX cameras traveled from the depths of the ocean to the peak of Mount Everest, resulting in a slew of forty-five-minute documentaries that were screened in science museums across the country. Even then, IMAX had their eyes on Hollywood, but it would take until the twenty-first century for the format to gain traction as a vehicle for mainstream narrative filmmaking. In the 2000s, the rise of digital formats meant that filmmakers no longer had to shoot on heavyweight IMAX cameras that used very expensive 70mm film stock. The smaller digital cameras, with their convenient computerized storage systems, made them more cost-effective than any analogue format, let alone IMAX. At the same time, IMAX themselves changed their projection standards, reducing the size and aspect ratio of their screens to license the system out to multiplexes across the country. This led to the rise of what film nerds derisively refer to as “LieMax”: IMAX-branded screens that were nowhere near as large as what you would find in a classic science museum IMAX. These LieMAX screens also had a more standard wide-screen shape , instead of the square shape that was IMAX’s calling card. The changes worked, turning IMAX from a curiosity for tourists and school groups into a central part of America’s cinema culture. Though the branding still focused on the size of the screen and the scale of the movies, the actual experience of IMAX became something closer to the best screen in your local multiplex than the enveloping, unique moviegoing experience you’d get at a Smithsonian or Kennedy Space Center IMAX theater. A key figure in that rise was Christopher Nolan himself. Nolan was one of the first filmmakers to embrace IMAX, shooting sequences in The Dark Knight with the format, and continuing to use IMAX on every film after that. The Odyssey has made history by becoming the first movie shot entirely on 70mm IMAX cameras. It’s clear that Nolan’s use of IMAX has had a profound effect on his filmmaking style. Comparing his early movies to his more recent work, Nolan’s IMAX period has led to a greater mastery of how to stage and block action scenes, more vivid and impressionistic imagery, and an epic grandeur and sweep. Nolan might never have become the filmmaker he is today, capable of driving millions of people to go see a biopic about a theoretical physicist, without IMAX. IMAX has been good for Nolan, and Nolan has been great for IMAX. The box office stats from The Odyssey are simply astonishing. Four weekends in, IMAX accounted for 43 percent of The Odyssey ’s domestic box office, despite making up just four hundred of nearly four thousand screens the movie played on. The numbers are even crazier for 70mm IMAX, the ultra-premium format that Nolan prefers, where the movie has made $27.6 million on the mere forty-one venues capable of screening the format. Tales from the 70mm IMAX screenings recall stories of seeing the Beatles live in 1964. People are traveling several hours , sneaking into screenings that have been sold out for months, and hauling themselves to the theater at 3 a.m. to see the movie in the best possible format. Why American Cinema Can’t Capitalize on IMAX’s Promise Viewers have spoken: they want to see big, original movies projected on film. Given the widespread demand for ultra-premium IMAX 70mm, the next steps should be obvious. Build more theaters — meet the demand by increasing supply. It’s clear that IMAX and their movie theater partners would stand to make a lot of money by opening more IMAX 70mm screens, and it would be great for film fans everywhere if more people had the opportunity to see big movies the way their filmmakers intended them to be seen. And yet, according to the CEO of IMAX , it’s not possible to build enough screens to meet demand. The reason doesn’t have to do with the size of the theaters, or even the lack of upcoming movies that use the format. Instead, according to IMAX CEO Richard Gelfond, “The problem is they haven’t made new IMAX film projectors in about fifty years.” The culprit turns out to be deindustrialization . The skilled labor required to make the specialized parts needed to run these complex machines simply doesn’t exist anymore, the kinds of jobs that have been offshored and automated away for decades. In laying off workers and closing factories, knowledge of how to build and maintain these machines has been lost to the point that, as the CEO confessed, no one knows how to make them anymore. The same issues apply to the operation end. Showing a movie in 70mm IMAX requires trained projectionists, which used to be a good-paying, high-skill, unionized job. Today’s digital systems, in contrast, merely require someone to push a button. It may have juiced profits in the short term, but all this automation and digitization has led to a long-term decline in the health of moviegoing itself. In their haste to crush a unionized workforce, theaters degraded their own product to the point where most screens offer a substandard experience at an inflated price, expecting families to spend over $100 to watch fuzzy, underlit images projected onto broken screens. To many, the true value of today’s IMAX experience comes in the company’s quality control. IMAX famously monitors every theater for picture and sound quality. Given that today most IMAX screens use digital projection for screens just slightly larger than the average theater, they effectively represent a surcharge on the parts of moviegoing that used to come for free: quality, clear image, and booming sound. But while technical issues are holding back the movie industry’s ability to show big, original movies in the best format, surely nothing is stopping them from still making those big, original movies, right? Unfortunately, even though this year’s box office is the result of a trend that has been growing for years, Hollywood remains terrified of originality. Large corporations, beholden to their shareholders, are forced to justify their big spends. It’s much easier for Wall Street to understand why a studio approved a Star Wars or DC Comics flop than an original one. While Nolan is certainly the top director in Hollywood when it comes to commercial appeal, he’s far from the only A-lister. And yet everyone else still finds themselves forced to play along with the studios’ IP fixation. Greta Gerwig will follow Barbie with two Chronicles of Narnia films, Denis Villeneuve is making a Dune sequel and a new James Bond movie, and Ryan Coogler’s next movie is Black Panther 3 . Despite the success of completely original movies like Sinners and Obsession , no one seems to be in a rush to give moviegoers more of what they’ve very clearly said they want: something they’ve never seen before. The American Theatrical Experience Is Likely to Get Worse So if giving customers what they actually want — more original movies in the best possible format — isn’t possible, how will everyone make money on this surge of interest? Here’s where things get dark, because if you can’t build more theaters, the industry will instead look to make more money off the theaters that already exist. Ideas floating around range from charging more for the best seats in a theater to increasing the upcharges for fancy formats to resale markets. Taking them one at a time, AMC has already floated a proposal for putting the best seats in their theaters behind a paywall, something that would represent an unprecedented shift in tiering the movie theater experience. As for increasing the format upcharges, moviegoers already pay extra to see a movie in IMAX, but as the weeks of sold-out Odyssey screenings show, the choked-off supply has led to a clear demand crisis, one that IMAX and movie theaters will be eager to profit from. Then there’s the question of resale. A year ago, as a publicity stunt, IMAX 70mm tickets went on sale for The Odyssey ’s opening weekend. This was highly unusual; while movie presales are happening earlier and earlier, The Odyssey had not even finished production when the tickets went on sale. No one even had any idea how long the movie was going to be, let alone if they would be free to see it at 7 p.m. on Friday a year in advance. The tickets sold out in seconds, and then many of them started appearing on eBay at inflated prices. Now with the movie in theaters, the process has been playing out again, as tickets go on sale, quickly sell out, and then appear on secondary resale sites. This is certainly something the movie theaters have been paying attention to. As anyone who tried to get tickets to The Odyssey knows, movie theater ticket sites are not currently prepared to handle a big crush of users at once. Many people have found it more efficient to travel to the theater in person and buy tickets there than to do it online. So if a redesign and upgrade of the online ticketing portals is already needed, could resale be on the way? It’s not totally off the table, with industry and business publications taking notice of the active secondary market for Odyssey tickets. If someone’s already making hundreds of dollars off resale, why not the theaters? The model for this sort of monetization already exists: just look at concert industry behemoth Live Nation Entertainment. Live Nation runs their own resale marketplace for concert tickets. They charge a fee for every transaction, meaning they receive a fee from a customer who buys a ticket, then another one when that customer sells the ticket to someone else. The system incentivizes Live Nation to encourage resale; they make more money off a ticket that’s sold to a scalper who then resells the ticket than they do if someone simply buys a ticket and attends a show. And because they double dip on fees, ticket prices on the resale market must be sold at a higher price to break even, meaning even someone trying to resell their ticket in good faith must charge a higher price to recoup the initial cost. Not coincidentally, Live Nation is one of the potential buyers for IMAX. What an IMAX Sale Could Look Like The success of The Odyssey has driven IMAX’s stock prices up at a very fortuitous moment. A few months ago, IMAX confirmed that they have been exploring a sale. To date, IMAX has been an independent company, meaning that every film studio and major theater chain has some kind of deal with IMAX. This hasn’t always been the case with Hollywood’s emerging technology. VistaVision, for example, was proprietary to Paramount while Dolby Cinemas, a LieMAX-style high-quality digital projection, are mostly in AMC cinemas in America. An IMAX sale would threaten to completely upend this fragile system. Right now, IMAX’s independence allows them to act as a sort of middleman, managing the competing agendas of different movie theater chains and studios. They can opt to prioritize movies that present the best spectacle for IMAX. That’s why, last weekend, every IMAX theater continued to show The Odyssey , rather than switching out that film for Spider-Man: Brand New Day . Even though the Spider-Man movie was new and a big hit, The Odyssey was filmed for IMAX; it presented a better filmgoing experience and thus had access to the screens. This could change under a new owner, especially given the simple logic of who would be interested in buying IMAX. A buyer would likely come from one of three places: a film studio, a theater chain, or private equity. Among the likely buyers for IMAX would be a movie studio like Disney. But IMAX falling into the hands of a studio would almost certainly lead to that studio’s movies receiving favorable IMAX placement. Indeed, many financial analysts have suggested Disney would be a likely buyer, precisely because their new Spider-Man and Avengers movies lost out on IMAX screens to The Odyssey and Dune: Part Three . Instead of prioritizing movies that were shot on IMAX 70mm film, conceived for an experience only possible in those theaters, a Disney-owned IMAX would prioritize their own films. Instead of The Odyssey playing to sold-out theaters for months, they might have been able to squeeze in two weeks between Moana and Spider-Man , meaning that millions of film fans would be deprived of the experience of seeing the movie as the director intended. A theater chain like AMC or Regal could purchase IMAX and preserve independence on this front, but that would lead to other issues. IMAX is currently a technology company whose tech is licensed by movie theaters. Virtually every major theater chain has some percentage of screens devoted to IMAX. If AMC bought IMAX, what would happen to all the other company’s IMAX screens? Currently, IMAX funds and assigns projectionists for major 70mm releases. Would an AMC-owned IMAX be as willing to help out a rival like Regal? Not only that, but IMAX has far more brand recognition than any individual theater chain. There’s a reason why movie posters say “See it in IMAX,” often in a bigger font than the title of the film itself. Would a theater be tempted to rebrand their entire chain as IMAX? That would risk further diluting an already diluted brand, squandering the goodwill that the IMAX experience has built up over the years. That leaves private equity, and the pages of Jacobin are littered with stories of what has happened to once-thriving businesses once they were acquired by private equity. Everything from increased ticket prices to pay-to-play to resale would be on the table, along with a gutting of the quality assurance at the heart of IMAX. That expensive process of monitoring every screen for quality simply wouldn’t fly with a cost-cutting mandate from a private equity firm. As for solutions, they’re few and far between. Given its vital role at the center of film in America, maintaining IMAX’s independence should be a central goal of any sale or merger. But the government will simply never step in to prioritize the health of an art form over the cynical profit calculations of a business sale. A strong union could fight back, but as discussed, the switch from film to digital decimated the unionized workforce that used to keep movie theaters running. The reality is that one technology company shouldn’t have this much control over the future of cinema. But there are options beyond IMAX and AMC. In addition to their IMAX screenings, The Odyssey , other major blockbusters like Sinners , and even prestige movies like Bugonia and The Brutalist have received releases in traditional 70mm and 35mm. While these formats don’t have the epic scale of a 70mm IMAX screening, they give the warm, vivid color and texture that comes with film projection. Most of these screenings take place in independent theaters, and all have a human projectionist monitoring the screening for quality control. In the end, however, these opportunities are harder and harder to find outside of major cities. For decades, cinema has thrived as an art form because of its accessibility. Cheap prices, mass production, and wide distribution of a top-quality experience are the reasons why film survived the Great Depression, the rise of television, and the age of streaming. The threat here is not one of technology or creativity but greed. As we’ve seen in other film industry news , the future of cinema is at the mercy of a few oligarchs, and while some filmgoers choose to root for “good” ones over “bad” ones, the reality is that any consolidation will further degrade an already fragile system.

articles.title: Centrists Are Still Defending California Billionaires
articles.author: Conor Lynch
articles.content: When California Democrats met last week for the party’s executive board meeting, the question on everyone’s mind was whether they would back Proposition 40, the onetime billionaire wealth tax that has split the party in recent months. With some of the most powerful Democrats in the state opposing the measure — including Gov. Gavin Newsom and his likely successor, Xavier Becerra — it was far from certain whether the board would support it. When it came to the floor for a vote, it fell just short of the 60 percent threshold required for endorsement. It was only after a second vote, along with a decisive show of support from veteran Rep. Maxine Waters, that the board narrowly endorsed the measure with 61.7 percent backing. The party’s endorsement gave Prop 40 a much-needed boost in the face of a billionaire-backed opposition that has already raised nearly $120 million and recently launched an $87 million ad blitz . It also defied the wishes of top California Democrats and underscored a widening rift between the party’s centrist leadership and its rank-and-file members. By endorsing the measure, the California Democratic Party aligned itself with the party’s base, which overwhelmingly backs the proposal in the polls. “Individual Democratic leaders may or may not have their own opinions but Voting Yes on Prop 40 is the official Democratic Party position,” said Will Rodriguez-Kennedy, chair of the San Diego County Democratic Party. This vote, he added, “indicates that the Democratic Party will take on the most powerful people out there to save Californian lives from the cruel healthcare cuts enacted by the Trump administration.” The endorsement of the billionaire wealth tax marks the latest sign of populism’s growing force inside the Democratic Party, which even the most vocal opponents of the proposal now seem to recognize. Governor Newsom, who mounted a sustained effort to kill the initiative before it got on the ballot, has since sought to qualify his stance ahead of a likely presidential campaign, framing his opposition as a disagreement over how to tax the ultrarich. In a video and Substack post published the day after the wealth tax officially made it onto the state’s ballot in late June, the outgoing California governor reiterated his opposition, criticizing the proposal’s spending priorities and warning that billionaires would flee the state if it passed. At the same time, Newsom insisted that he supports reining in the billionaire class, but that it must be done at the federal level. The “fight against concentrated wealth is a national fight,” declared the governor, before laying out an alternative set of proposals under the banner of a “national billionaires’ tax.” Contrary to some reporting in the press , Newsom did not propose a national wealth tax, which progressives also support. Instead, he offered a set of reforms aimed at closing loopholes in the tax code, raising the top rates on current taxes, and creating what he calls a “minimum tax on billionaires.” Importantly, these proposals would not target wealth but income , thus capturing only a fraction of the annual gains that make up billionaires’ true earnings. As tax expert Gabriel Zucman, who helped craft the California wealth tax, observed in a post on X, Newsom’s proposals would “do almost nothing to curb the explosion of the wealth and power of America’s oligarchs.” The “Pragmatic Populist” Playbook The dispute over the billionaire wealth tax in California foreshadows a broader debate that Democrats will have in the years ahead. As pressure mounts to tax America’s oligarchs, bold proposals like the wealth tax will likely continue to grow in popularity. This presents a conundrum for the party’s centrists, especially those with higher political ambitions. Newsom’s effort to repackage himself as a kind of pragmatic populist ahead of a likely presidential run offers a preview of how establishment Democrats will attempt to appease the party’s increasingly populist base without alienating the big donors who still finance their campaigns. If the debate in California is any guide, centrist Democrats will frame their opposition to proposals like the wealth tax in strictly pragmatic terms, focusing on unintended economic consequences or the institutional challenges of enacting such policies. In the Golden State, Newsom and other Democratic critics have mostly argued that the proposal would drive wealthy residents out of the state and thus erode its tax base and long-term revenue. Nationally, the “pragmatic” critique will likely center on the constitutional challenges that a federal wealth tax would inevitably face. These criticisms are not entirely groundless. It is true, for example, that a state wealth tax would be difficult to administer and that the wealthy are highly mobile, especially at the state level. While narratives about wealthy residents fleeing states due to high taxes are greatly exaggerated — often built on anecdotes rather than hard data, which shows relatively little tax-related migration — the California wealth tax lacks any real historical precedent. Though structured as a onetime retroactive tax to curb avoidance and limit economic fallout, it’s not unreasonable to assume that some of the state’s wealthiest residents will leave if the measure passes (whether that’s such a bad thing is a different question). While a national wealth tax would be far more difficult for the wealthy to escape by simply packing up and moving, it faces its own serious obstacles. Indeed, a straightforward tax on wealth would almost certainly be struck down by today’s Supreme Court, where conservative justices have indicated they would rule against any “direct tax” that isn’t narrowly construed as an income tax. These challenges are real and shouldn’t be casually dismissed by wealth tax proponents. At the same time, the ostensibly more “practical” alternatives sold by centrists like Newsom would do little to confront the very problems that proposals like a wealth tax are designed to remedy, from extreme inequality and outsize billionaire power to persistent tax avoidance at the top. Take the proposal to eliminate the “buy, borrow, die” loophole, which first gained notoriety in 2021 when a ProPublica report revealed how some of the country’s wealthiest men routinely avoided taxable income by taking out low-interest loans backed by their assets. While simply taxing wealth or unrealized gains would automatically render this strategy obsolete, centrist Democrats have rallied around a more technocratic fix that would avoid dramatic changes to the current tax code. The most popular proposal is to simply tax loans as if they were capital gains. In June, another presidential hopeful aiming to occupy the “pragmatic populist” lane, Arizona senator Ruben Gallego, introduced a bill that would treat such loans as “realization events” for those with assets over $1 billion. In theory, this would eliminate the tax incentive to take out loans in the first place. There are a few issues with this approach. For one, it’s unclear how much better it would actually fare in the courts. According to Brian Galle, a professor of tax law at Berkeley, proposals to tax borrowing would “face constitutional challenges that are not especially different from those facing wealth taxes more generally.” Though Galle argues that it would be constitutional “on the best reading of the existing law,” this wouldn’t prevent the Supreme Court from trying “very hard to find ways to strike it down.” The bigger problem is that a tax on loans simply wouldn’t raise much revenue from billionaires. Recent research has found that annual borrowing from the wealthiest American households represents just a fraction of their total income when untaxed (i.e., unrealized) earnings are included. “[It] turns out that when you are super-rich you already have enough cash flow to fund most of your private jet and megayacht purchases, even if that is a tiny share of your overall wealth,” noted Galle. In practical terms, this means that eliminating the loophole would hardly touch the real income of the ultrarich. In a column , Rep. Ro Khanna claimed that a tax on loans would generate just one forty-fourth of what his and Bernie Sanders’s proposed 5 percent wealth tax on billionaires would raise. Taxing Wealth Without Calling It That If centrist proposals fail because they don’t target the true source of billionaire wealth and power, progressive plans like Sanders and Khanna’s national wealth tax would likely fail for the opposite reason: they target it so directly that the conservative majority on the Supreme Court would rule it unconstitutional. A truly pragmatic approach would avoid the legal pitfalls of a direct wealth tax while still finding a way to tax the wealth of the ultrarich. For a time, taxing unrealized gains was seen as a somewhat more viable option, since it could be plausibly framed as an income tax. That idea sat at the heart of the Biden administration’s “billionaire minimum income tax,” which applied to households with more than $100 million in assets. Since then, the constitutional prospects of this approach have also dimmed considerably. Galle, who helped craft the Biden proposal, noted that it was developed before a Supreme Court ruling in 2024 where conservative justices signaled they would deem a tax on unrealized gains unconstitutional as well. In a monograph published earlier this year, Galle outlined a new plan that he argues could sidestep these constitutional hurdles while still meaningfully taxing the ultrarich. Galle’s framework, the Fair Share Tax (FAST), offers a sophisticated work-around to the Supreme Court’s strict interpretation of the “realization rule,” under which only realized gains qualify as taxable income. Rather than taxing wealth or unrealized gains, FAST would tax gains only at realization but impose an additional interest charge equal to the asset’s annual return, making it far more expensive to hold assets indefinitely. As Galle explained to me, FAST would “tax investment assets when they are sold, but [also] adjust the tax rate that individuals pay so that after paying the tax they are left with the same amount they would have held if they had been taxed annually.” In his telling, this would generate the “revenue and economic effects of a wealth-type tax with the administrative ease and constitutional compatibility of a traditional income tax.” Under the current tax code, any investment gains that aren’t officially realized during the owner’s life are effectively wiped out at death for tax purposes, leaving heirs with a mostly tax-free inheritance (hence the final step of the “buy, borrow, die” strategy). To eliminate this loophole, known as the “step-up basis” rule, tax experts have suggested treating death itself as a realization event. This could be paired with the replacement of the estate tax with an inheritance tax to be paid by heirs. Galle’s plan would eliminate the step-up basis loophole and pass all the gains made during the life of the investment onto the inheritors, accumulating even more interest over time. He also proposes an additional tax on heirs when they sell their inherited property that would kick in at $15 million in property gains. Ahead of the 2028 election, a real debate is needed on how to tax the top 0.1 percent in a way that is both effective and workable. With a judicial branch openly hostile to such efforts, the more creative solutions there are on the table, the better. But despite recent proclamations about the dangers of concentrated wealth and spiraling inequality, centrist Democrats like Newsom seem largely committed to symbolic gestures that would do little to curb the power or fortunes of the billionaire class. It falls to the Left to articulate a genuinely pragmatic brand of populism instead.

articles.title: Why the Gig Economy Won’t Call Workers Employees
articles.author: Paul Osterman
articles.content: As gig work has expanded from a marginal feature of the labor market into a significant one, a question that once seemed narrow and technical has taken on broad consequences: What does it mean to be an employee? The answer shapes whether a worker can join a union, whether they are owed overtime, whether they have recourse if injured on the job, and whether they can collect unemployment if the platform cuts them off. Employers have strong financial incentives to classify workers as independent contractors rather than employees, and many have pursued that classification aggressively, even where the practical reality of the work relationship closely resembles traditional employment. The disputes that have followed, in courts, in regulatory agencies, and in legislatures, reveal not just a legal ambiguity but a policy system struggling to keep pace with how work has actually changed. To see why defining who is an employee is complicated, consider the disputes around ride-sharing services. Uber, working hard to avoid any ruling that its drivers are employees, calls the people behind the wheel “driver-partners,” but this is an odd use of the term partner . The CEO of Uber earned $24 million in 2022, while only 13 percent of Uber drivers in 2021 earned $30,000 or more. This difference among “partners” is remarkable compared to, say, law firms, where a top partner in a big New York firm earns only about twice as much as an average partner. Presumably, Uber uses the term as a signal of its insistence that the drivers are freelancers and not employees, but it is surprising that it can do this with a straight face. Rhetoric aside, employee status for Uber drivers is complicated. For most drivers, the job is a part-time supplement to another standard job they hold. In a survey of Uber drivers, Jonathan Gruber reported that 45 percent earned less than $5,000 from all app jobs and only about a quarter earned $20,000 or more annually from all apps. In any three-month period, the survey found, only 22 percent worked more than twenty hours a week for four consecutive weeks. While most drivers are clearly doing the work part-time, for a nontrivial fraction, driving is their only and main livelihood. And the ride-share companies exert considerable control over how the drivers do their work. The importance of this point will become apparent when the relevant law is described below. One might argue that the amount of effort and focus of advocates on the classification of gig workers seems disproportionate to the importance of these gig jobs in the labor markets. That figure is 1.9 percent of the workforce according to my estimate, an estimate that is consistent with that of other researchers . This would be a misreading of what is at stake. Many employers outside of ride-sharing are pushing against employee status, and what we see is essentially an effort to chip away at the boundaries. Consider that FedEx doesn’t seem to stop looking for ways to classify more of its workforce as freelancers. Another example along the same lines is Amazon Flex, a service by which drivers use their own trucks to deliver packages, but do so under tight control by Amazon. Yet the company insists that they are freelancers. Likewise, Walmart is building its own delivery system, called Spark, which relies on freelancers who are under tight corporate control. Indeed, as the Wall Street Journal reported , “Today tens of thousands of Spark drivers, who aren’t Walmart employees and are paid by the delivery, make the majority of the retailer’s same-day deliveries. Walmart pays Spark drivers about $10, plus tip, to pick up orders from Walmart workers at stores, and sometimes collect items from shelves.” Sometimes these efforts to play the classification game are almost comical: for example, a Las Vegas casino I interviewed dressed its cocktail waitresses as comic-strip characters so that it could claim them as performers rather than employees. A similar tactic was addressed by the courts when reality television shows were compelled to classify their contestants as employees. If boundaries were weakened, it is easy to imagine employers in other industries similarly hiving off pieces of their workforces into freelance status. A Possible Legal Solution At the federal level, there are currently two somewhat different legal tests for defining who is an employee: the standard used by the Department of Labor’s Wage and Hours Division, the agency responsible for interpreting and enforcing the Fair Labor Standards Act; and the standard used by the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB). These differing standards rest on different underlying bodies of law. The NLRB is compelled to rely on common law (that is, court decisions on prior cases, not all of which are consistent with each other) because the statutory language does not define employee , whereas the Fair Labor Standards Act language does define “to employ” as meaning “to suffer or permit work.” This language is seen as broader than the common law framing and so opens the door to more aggressive treatment of ride-sharing and to joint-employment liability. As a practical matter, the two standards often overlap, and each depends on a list of job features such as degree of employer control, the scope of whatever discretion the worker has, the length of the relationship, and whether it appears the individual is in business for him or herself. Because the list is long under either of the standards, it becomes a matter of judgment and dispute over how to measure each factor and which to weigh most heavily. Indeed, in 1968, the Supreme Court unhelpfully ruled that there is no shorthand formula or magic phrase that can be applied to find the answer, and instead, all the features of the relationship must be assessed and weighed, with no one factor being decisive. What is important is that the total factual context be assessed. The consequence is seemingly endless confusion and contestation. The challenges arise in part from inconsistent court rulings, but most problematic are the constantly shifting administrative agency interpretations, which cycle back and forth depending on the political winds. After the Obama administration adopted, in the Department of Labor’s Wage and Hours Division, a broad interpretation of the definition of employee status, the first Trump administration rescinded it and narrowed the definition by putting a heavy emphasis on the entrepreneurial opportunities of the worker. (Hence, an Uber driver could be considered an entrepreneur and therefore not an employee.) The Biden administration then returned to the Obama view, and at this writing the new Trump administration had not yet but was expected to undo the Biden rules. The same back-and-forth occurs with labor law. The National Labor Relations Board in the Obama years ruled in FedEx Home Delivery that drivers were employees, whereas in 2019, under Donald Trump, a new board considering SuperShuttle DFW , with essentially the same fact pattern, ruled that drivers were freelancers. All of this confusion is complicated even more because some important protective legislation, such as Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, offers no definition of employee status. The ideal solution would begin with legislative clarification of how to define an employee. A straightforward approach would be federal adoption of the so-called ABC rule, already in use by over thirty states to define employee status for state employment rules and for programs related to minimum wages, unemployment insurance, and workers’ compensation. This rule makes the assumption that everyone is an employee unless the employer can prove otherwise, and to succeed, that employer needs affirmative evidence on three criteria: that the work is done without the direction and control of the employer, that the work is outside the usual scope of the employer’s business, and that the person doing the work has their own independent business or trade doing that kind of work. Simple and clear as this might seem, getting such a thing through Congress seems impossible, and in fact, an effort to do just this failed when the reform bill titled the 2021 Protecting the Right to Organize Act died in Congress. Absent a legislative remedy, the line between employee status and freelancer status will continue to be disputed and uncertain, with the resolution lying less in thinking about the law and more in thinking about who sits on the courts and in the White House.
